newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Small change agreed on Australia Telstra bill.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Small change agreed on Australia Telstra bill.

text.p: Key Australian Independent Senator Brian Harradine said he and the government had agreed on a small amendment to the bill to partially privatise telecoms carrier Telstra Corp.
Harradine said he wanted the commencement date of the bill delayed so that there could be debate on the method of privatisation before the sale went ahead.
"I will be preparing such an amendment," he told the Senate.
The joint amendment means that, to some extent, there has been a meeting of minds between the government and Harradine, one of two Independents whose votes will determine the bill.
Earlier, the Independents sided with the government to prevent the bill being killed off immediately after the debate stage (the second reading).

It was then being briefly sidetracked by an attempt to delay consideration of the bill until next year -- again defeated with Independent support -- and has now progressed to the amendment stage (the committee of the whole).
The amendment stage might change details of the bill. After that, the Senate will finally vote on it in its amended form.
The government hopes for a final vote later on Thursday but at 0145 GMT (12.45 p.m.) the Senate stopped for lunch.
The government also sweetened its lure for the Independent votes on Thursday.

First, it said it would increase the environmental repair fund to be created from the sale proceeds to A$1.1 billion from A$1.0 billion. Tasmania, Harradine's home state, would get priority, Communications Minister Richard Alston said.

Second, Alston said the government would create a A$250 million fund to develop telecoms infrastructure outside of main cities, answering a stated concern of the other Independent, Mal Colston, who is based in Queensland.
Colston has been more positive on Thursday about eventually supporting the bill than Harradine, who is always non-committal before most votes.
Harradine has merely said that he would vote for the bill if his concerns were met -- which has always been his position.
But Colston said on Thursday that the government had a electoral mandate for the privatisation and that he expected his concerns would be met.
The government hopes to raise about A$8 billion by selling a third of Telstra, Australia's biggest company.
The government is two votes short of a majority in the Senate and among non-government senators only the Independents will countenance the privatisation.
